📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations. Momoa, who is of Native American descent on his mother's side, made his directorial debut with "Road to Paloma," which managed a sort of okay 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. Eight years later, he helped oversee another film centered on Native American heritage, this time in the form of a retelling of the legend of Willie Boy.

This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century. The pair absconded but were found and separated by their families. After Willie Boy moved to Banning, California, Carlota soon followed. But her father, William Mike, disapproved of the couple reuniting. He ended up dead, possibly due to having been intentionally shot by Willie Boy or as the result of an accident. After this began what's been called "the last Western Manhunt" in which Willie Boy was pursued by a Sheriff and his small posse over roughly 600 miles.

The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the big screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman. It was ultimately overshadowed by the actor's other Western from 1969: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid." In 2022, however, Momoa, writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett, and director Christian Camargo took another shot at adapting the same story in a very different way with "The Last Manhunt." If you'd like to see how it turned out, the film is currently streaming for free on Tubi.

Jason Momoa has a few underrated projects, but "The Last Manhunt" seemed more personal. According to Variety, the "Aquaman" star heard the story of Willie Boy while in the Joshua Tree area, where he owns a home. He and writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett then developed the story, even meeting with direct descendants of Carlotta's family. The result was a version of the legend based on the Chemehuevi's oral tradition. As Sibbet told Variety, "This is a living story for the Chemehuevi people. It has a special place for them. So we can honor their oral traditions by just listening to them.".

Industry observers note that momoa brought in Christian Camargo to direct, with whom he starred in the Apple TV series "See." Camargo previously wrote and directed 2013's "Days and Nights," which was based on Anton Chekhov's play "The Seagull" and boasted an impressive cast including Mark Rylance, William Hurt, and Ben Whishaw. Unfortunately, Camargo failed to do the Russian playwright's source material proud. "Days and Nights" presently sits at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics ripping into the drama for having nothing to say.

Recent findings suggest that all of which makes "The Last Manhunt" seem like an absolute triumph in comparison. The film stars Martin Sensmeier as Willie and Mainei Kinimaka as Carlotta, who trek across the desert after the death of Carlotta's father. They're pursued by Sheriff Wilson (Camargo) and a small group of indigenous people who want Willie to face justice for the killing. As the manhunt goes on, the ever more tragic consequences pile up. Momoa also appears in the film as Massive Jim, a Native member of the posse. But he's only in a handful of scenes and isn't given much to do.

"The Last Manhunt" didn't make much of an impact upon its 2022 release. After debuting at the first ever Pioneertown International Film Festival, it received distribution by Saban Films. But its limited theatrical release in November 2022 came and went and the film has just sort of languished on digital platforms ever since.

According to recent reports, thankfully, it's now on Tubi and is worth a watch if you're a Western fan. A 20% Rotten Tomatoes score probably isn't the best selling point, however. Luke Y. Thompson of the AV Club gave "The Last Manhunt" credit for "great visuals and the best of intentions" but ultimately found it to be little more than "a basic posse movie" that's "not exciting enough to just do that well." Catey Sullivan of the Chicago Reader, on the other hand, praised the film for "reclaiming the narrative of a Native hero" and delivering a story that "is at once an epic romance and gripping thriller." There's also plenty of acting talent on display. Alongside Martin Sensmeier and Mainei Kinimaka as the leads and Jason Momoa's brief appearances, there's Lily Gladstone as Carlotta's mother Marie, Zahn McClarnon as her father, William Johnson, as well as Wade Williams and Raoul Max Trujillo as trackers in pursuit of the couple.

Industry observers note that so, while "The Last Manhunt" is far from one of the best Westerns of the 21st Century, there's enough here for fans of the genre. Those interested to see whether Momoa and his cohorts managed to finally do justice to the Willie Boy legend should also find "The Last Manhunt" worthwhile. The film is available to stream on Tubi right now.

What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • According to recent reports, to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

According to recent reports, to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro stated. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro mentioned. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Industry observers note that hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The crucial part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro stated, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I swiftly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

It has been revealed that in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and mentioned, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

Recent findings suggest that “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro stated. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

According to recent reports, chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Latest York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

In a recent development, the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that growing up around performers, storytelling was always central to Emma's life. Add in a nerdy older brother who introduced her to Marvel at far too young an age, and her love for entertainment led her to pursue a Journalism degree at Indiana University, where she discovered her passion for entertainment reporting. She spent nearly one year in Los Angeles covering industry stories and fully immersing herself in the world of entertainment media.

When two of Hollywood's biggest directors sit down together, unexpected ideas are bound to come up.

It has been revealed that christopher Nolan's adaptation of The Odyssey follows Odysseus' journey home after the Trojan War. The movie stars Matt Damon as Odysseus alongside a star-studded ensemble including Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, and Charlize Theron. However, Steven Spielberg believes another story from Greek mythology could be worth exploring.

According to The Playlist, Spielberg playfully encouraged Nolan to adapt The Iliad, Homer's companion epic to The Odyssey. The suggestion came during a November 17 post-screening Q&A at the DGA Theater in Los Angeles, where Spielberg praised Nolan's filmmaking before proposing another adaptation:.

"The only other thing I want to say, not to challenge you or anything, but there's always 'The Iliad.'".

"No pressure, no pressure. But this could be the most successful movie in history that never had a sequel.".

Nolan laughed at the suggestion, replying, "I think now you're advocating for Universal." Spielberg responded that he was speaking on behalf of Universal Pictures executives Donna Langley and Peter Cramer, adding, "And me too.".

Interestingly, Nolan previously had an opportunity to adapt The Iliad, the companion epic to The Odyssey.The filmmaker was originally attached to direct Troy, the 2004 historical epic inspired by Homer's poem. However, Wolfgang Petersen ultimately directed the movie, which starred Brad Pitt as Achilles.

During the conversation, Nolan reflected on his previous attachment to direct Troy before The Odyssey, revealing that an idea he developed for the movie remained with him for more than two decades. The director had envisioned an image of the Trojan horse buried in sand, comparing it to the Statue of Liberty in Planet of the Apes.

Industry observers note that nolan's interest in Greek mythology also dates back to childhood. The director previously revealed that one of his earliest memories was watching a school production of Ulysses when he was just five or six years old. His brother, Jonathan Nolan, also praised The Odyssey as an incredible achievement, revealing that the two had discussed Christopher's approach to adapting Homer's epic.

Recent findings suggest that although The Iliad and The Odyssey are closely connected, the former would not be a traditional sequel. The Iliad centers on events during the Trojan War, particularly the conflict involving Achilles and Agamemnon, while The Odyssey follows the aftermath through Odysseus' journey home.

Recent findings suggest that spielberg's suggestion follows the enormous box office success of The Odyssey, which has grossed over $1.8 billion worldwide. The film became both Nolan's and Universal Pictures' highest-grossing release of all time, while also breaking the record for the highest-grossing R-rated movie worldwide. With the film's historic performance, another Homer adaptation could be an appealing opportunity for Universal.

Sources indicate that coming from a filmmaker behind some of the best movies of all time, such as Jaws, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Jurassic Park, and Schindler's List, Spielberg's suggestion carries weight.

In a recent development, however, Nolan has not declared plans to adapt The Iliad. His producing partner Emma Thomas recently revealed that the director is considering ideas for his next projects on what movies that should come after The Odyssey, although nothing has been decided. Whether Spielberg's encouragement will influence Nolan's next move remains to be seen.

The Odyssey is presently available to rent or purchase on multiple digital platforms.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is a 2026 adaptation of Homer's epic poem, chronicling Odysseus's treacherous journey home from the Trojan War.

Latest Update: Sorry, Vice City, but You’re the Most Boring Part of GTA 6

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Grand Theft Auto 6 was first declared, fans were thrilled at the prospect of returning to Vice City.
  • According to recent reports, I don’t mean to say that Vice City sucks — far from it!
  • I blame GTA 6’s opening chapter for spoiling me rotten.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Grand Theft Auto 6 was first declared, fans were thrilled at the prospect of returning to Vice City. The Miami-inspired location has always been one of the series’ most memorable locations, its neon-lit streets standing in contrast to the grittiness of Liberty City. While I was as excited as anyone to go clubbing and spend some time on the beach, after 70 hours, GTA 6 has struck me with one surprise thought: Vice City is the least interesting part of Leonida.

According to recent reports, I don’t mean to say that Vice City sucks — far from it! It’s an immaculately designed video game city with more environmental diversity in any given corner than some open-world games fit into an entire map. The fact that it’s one of my least favorite places to spend time is more a testament to every other location in GTA 6’s Florida-inspired world. From small towns to the deep wilderness, every corner of Leonida is a delight to discover because every area feels so different.

I blame GTA 6’s opening chapter for spoiling me rotten. Jason and Lucia’s story begins in the Leonida Keys, a brilliantly constructed introductory area that I fell in love with instantly. As someone who is fascinated by the Florida Keys, the real islands that the location is based on, I was thrilled to find a digital space that so accurately captured a genuinely surreal part of America. The real Keys feel like an isolated nation, densely packing stores and suburbs onto narrow islands. The Leonida Keys feel both like an idyllic vacation hideaway and a mundane suburb, which gives GTA 6’s opening chapter such a distinct feel from the rest of the game. The small town nature of it makes for one of my favorite chunks of any GTA game.

It has been revealed that even after getting out of the Leonida Keys, it’s still a while before you get to Vice City. First, Jason and Lucia spend a stint upstate hopping around some small towns separated by vast farmland. Port Gellhorn has the feel of an industrial town, the kind of place that’s lined with used car lots. Some great action set pieces come out of that setup; one time I busted up a well-guarded abandoned bowling alley and wound up in a gritty gang shootout.

Sources indicate that way south of there, you’ll find Capri, another highlight. The squeaky-clean upper-class town is full of boutique clothing stores and high-end cafes. When Jason and Lucia arrive there, they are immediately profiled by street cops who clock them as poor outsiders who don’t belong in town. It stings considering how hard up for cash the two are when they get there, which turns the town itself into one of GTA 6’s greatest antagonists. Screw this place!

Industry observers note that even the stretches of map that seem empty at a glance are fascinating. Some of my favorite moments so far have been spent in Lummox County, which is largely made up of woods and mountains (despite IRL Florida not technically having those). Some of the best date spots and activities are up there, hidden alongside hiking trails. It’s also home to some true weirdos, like a group of “conservationist” gun nuts who say they are controlling the ecosystem by shooting at invasive lizards. Those weirdo discoveries make what could have been a dull, empty area into a place that I keep feeling compelled to bike around.

Industry observers note that between all of those areas, there are so many little pockets of the map to love. Hullet Marsh hides one of the game’s weirdest secrets amid the alligators. Tiny islands like Belpoint are quaint little escapes worth seeking out. Even unassuming stretches of road, like the area under Buckskin Swamp, will lead you to decaying mini-golf courses that make you feel like you’re in a state with a lot of history to it. I’ve seen every corner of the map, and very little of it has felt like a waste of exploration.

It has been revealed that vice City is excellent too, of course. It’s a perfect representation of Miami, right down to the hotel pools that I’ve sat by while visiting my brother, who lives there. Vice Beach is a highlight, and the various Keys around the city give the area a lot of diversity. It’s more just that I expected all of that. I know that Rockstar can get the hustle and bustle of cities right, because I’ve been playing GTA games since I was a kid. It’s more exciting to see GTA 6 branch out into more intimate towns and figure out how to make those just as exciting without the sports cars and nightclubs. GTA games have explored these spaces before, but the sheer mass of them here helps Leonida feel like a fully realized state with its own economic and political nuances from region to region.

My relationship to Vice City as it stands is similar to the relationship I have to Manhattan as a Brooklynite. It’s work island. Clock in, make some money, and leave the city limits at sunset to actually live a little. I’ll remember my mini-golf games more than the hours I spent sitting in traffic on Vice City’s freeways.

Sources indicate that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Industry observers note that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be crucial for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

In a recent development, “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

According to recent reports, “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Sources indicate that still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

In a recent development, “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado noted. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford noted, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other massive studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

In a recent development, “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really rapidly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” mentioned Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

According to recent reports, “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” noted Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

Recent findings suggest that “People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” remarked Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

Industry observers note that one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Industry observers note that directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

In a recent development, what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, promptly says he fell short in “Obsession.”.

In a recent development, “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” remarked Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

According to recent reports, as Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

It has been revealed that “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Dragon Quest franchise has been around for longer than some of us have been alive, and its first entry in 1986 was one of the JRPG genre’s pioneers. Over the years, the launch of a fresh title in the series has been a massive deal, especially in Japan. Before players missed work to play Grand Theft Auto 6, they were using sick days to topple wicked dragonlords.

Industry observers note that in North America, Dragon Warrior 7 (the last entry in the series to bear that localized title), arrived after two previous installments weren’t released outside Japan. Interest had waned. When the game hit stores on Nov. 1, 2001, it was as difficult to find as its NES predecessors had been. And when loyal fans finally tracked it down, we wound up being disappointed. But over the years, Square Enix has made some adjustments and tried again on multiple occasions. Happily, each upcoming release of Dragon Quest 7 gets better than the one before it.

It has been revealed that dragon Quest 7 spent a long time in development and arrived late enough in the original PlayStation’s life cycle that it felt decidedly old-fashioned by the time any of us got the chance to play it. The visuals were a step above anything the Super Nintendo offered, finally rendered in 3D with a camera that players could rotate. But the experience still felt a bit like a step back compared to the flatter but more detailed environments of late PS1-era games like Final Fantasy 9. In some respects, it was a relic from a time many players had moved on from.

The quest’s opening hours didn’t correct that first impression. I remember playing for three hours without encountering a single enemy mob, which just felt odd. In the typical Dragon Quest game from years prior, you could head outside the castle walls within a few short minutes. An hour into the adventure, you would have already battled dozens or even hundreds of monsters and leveled up your characters several times. Instead, I had to spend that time solving tedious puzzles.

Sources indicate that slow opening hours eventually gave way to a lengthy quest with plenty of appeal, but I didn’t actually stick around to experience those later events until Dragon Quest 7: Fragments of the Forgotten Past released on the 3DS on Sep. 16, 2016 in the West. Despite making its debut on portable hardware, the new release offered a superior way to experience the adventure.

The single change I appreciated most was an update to the formerly tedious first few hours of play. The introductory dungeon, with all of its levers and backtracking, was gone. Introductory areas still ate up more time than I was accustomed to, but they fit within a single gaming session and left me with time — and enthusiasm — to progress to more interesting activities.

The 3DS version offered other enhancements, as well. The bottom screen provided a helpful glow when the player approached stone tablet shards, a major component of progression. Players had a lot less guesswork to find essential items, a smart adjustment that eliminated a lot of pointless frustration.

Recent findings suggest that another new feature recapped the story, in case players stepped away for a few days, weeks, or longer. Accessible from the pause menu, a chronological log listed every major event that had occurred, along with hints about where to go next. (Later games in the series, all the way up to Dragon Quest 11, would keep this addition.) While exploring, party members might also offer suggestions if consulted, sparing players from some of the ambiguity that had been a franchise staple since its first installment.

Recent findings suggest that quality-of-life enhancements didn’t stop there, either. The game also introduced enemy mobs players could see in the field as they explored. Leveling up required less grinding, and menus were modified and streamlined. A map on the bottom screen made it easy to spot nearby points of interest. Most importantly, players could make a quick save outside of churches if they needed to stop playing suddenly. For a portable game, that option was a must.

According to recent reports, dragon Quest 7 on the 3DS remained the best way to play the game for a decade, until Dragon Quest 7 Reimagined launched in February 2026. Available on Switch, Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X, the updated take on the classic adventure introduced a breathtaking new art style. Presented like a diorama, the gorgeous visuals paired nicely with quality voice acting to bring the world’s story to life like never before.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The newest release also introduced new changes to the character vocation system, allowing party members to adopt two vocations at once and gain mastery in both of them. Changing a class no longer required a time-consuming visit to Alltrades Abbey, either. And on the world map, striking weaker monsters defeated them automatically with lesser rewards, a welcome compromise that eliminated the need to endure tedious skirmishes. There were other changes, as well, including multiple difficulty presets, a shared inventory, and auto-revive after battle for party members who perished in the fight.

It has been revealed that for RPG fans in 2026, these were smart adjustments. Few players appreciate busy work and random encounters that slow the pace more than necessary. It’s good to see developers revisiting past triumphs and modernizing them for contemporary audiences to enjoy. If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again. It certainly worked for Dragon Quest 7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The director behind one of Star Wars' most controversial sequels gives an enhancement about his future with the beloved science fiction franchise.

Recent findings suggest that released in 2017, The Last Jedi served as the second installment in the Star Wars sequel trilogy, following 2015's The Force Awakens. The film continued the stories of Rey, Kylo Ren, Finn, and Poe Dameron while bringing Luke Skywalker back into the picture. Despite receiving positive reviews from many critics, the sequel generated mixed feelings among fans, especially about the characters and storylines.

In a recent development, now, Rian Johnson has addressed the possibility of returning to the Star Wars universe nearly a decade after directing Star Wars: The Last Jedi. Although he currently has no aims to direct another installment in a galaxy far, far away, he is still interested in revisiting Star Wars if the right opportunity comes along.

In an interview with IndieWire at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, Johnson discussed his relationship with the franchise and whether another Star Wars project could be in his future. The director explained that he is at the moment busy developing his own original projects but is still open to the idea of doing another Star Wars project. He also noted that his love for the franchise has only grown since The Last Jedi.

Recent findings suggest that johnson also praised Lucasfilm's creative team and leadership, including Dave Filoni, who worked with him on The Last Jedi. His comments imply that he does have a good professional relationship with the studio despite not having directed another installment and that he is not closing the door on the Star Wars franchise for good.

Industry observers note that however, this should not be taken as a confirmation that there is another movie with Johnson in the works. The director did not announce a newly introduced Star Wars movie and didn't speak about any negotiations with Lucasfilm. His response is simply stating that he has not ruled out returning to the franchise.

Johnson's latest statement comes nine years after Lucasfilm unveiled that he would develop an entirely new Star Wars trilogy. In November 2017, the studio confirmed that Johnson would helm three films that were independent of the main Skywalker saga. He was expected to write and direct the first installment, with Ram Bergman attached as a producer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • In a recent development, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

In a recent development, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he mentioned through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I mentioned, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

It has been revealed that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he mentioned. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Recent findings suggest that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

Recent findings suggest that how’s his French? “Zero,” he stated. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” noted Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” mentioned Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

It has been revealed that one serious problem for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he mentioned. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

It has been revealed that and Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Industry observers note that was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he noted. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he mentioned, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

Sources indicate that when people talk about Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson today, the spotlight is usually on his blockbuster career. Since his film debut in The Mummy Returns back in 2001, he’s become one of the most bankable stars in Hollywood, anchoring franchises like Fast & Furious and Jumanji, voicing Disney favorites as he does in Moana, and exploring dramatic work in The Smashing Machine. But while he was dominating the box office, Johnson also made a detour into television that gave him room to show a different side of himself.

It has been revealed that that detour was HBO's Ballers, which premiered in 2015 and ran for five seasons. Following Johnson as a retired football player turned financial manager, the series was a quiet game-changer. It proved he could carry a character-driven drama, dig into complex storylines, and show range far beyond action and comedy. While Ballers never reached the cultural relevance of Succession or Game of Thrones, it carved out a loyal fanbase and gave Johnson the opportunity to show his talent ranged much further than charisma and muscles.

Ballers is sort of like Entourage in the world of sports, but Johnson’s Spencer Strasmore is far more layered than that shorthand suggests. A former NFL star forced into retirement by injuries, Spencer reinvented himself as a financial manager for current players. That setup opened the door to endless drama, comedy, and scandal as he tried to guide his clients through the pitfalls of fame, wealth, and the bad decisions that often came with both.

Recent findings suggest that at its best, Ballers used the world of sports to explore bigger challenges. It spotlighted the dangers of concussions and player safety, the financial risks of sudden wealth, and the sacrifices athletes make to keep playing the game they love. While the show had plenty of Miami flash and glamour, it never shied away from the painful reality of what happens when the spotlight fades. Spencer’s own demons, haunted by concussions and desperate to stay relevant, grounded the story and gave Johnson one of his most complex roles on screen.

Recent findings suggest that for audiences who only knew him as “The Rock” or as the face of blockbuster tentpoles, his role in Ballers was a revelation. Johnson brought surprising vulnerability beneath the swagger, delivering a performance that balanced confidence with self-doubt. And yes, he looked great in those suits, but it wasn’t just another cool-guy role for the bona fide movie star. It was proof he could anchor a drama with real emotional depth.

Sources indicate that when Ballers premiered, Johnson was already a global star, but his filmography leaned heavily on action tentpoles and family comedies. He was bankable, but not necessarily considered versatile. Playing Spencer across five seasons gave him the chance to shift that perception, proving he could handle long-form storytelling and layered character work that his usual projects didn’t always allow. Johnson wasn't just coasting on his charm, playing a character who was constantly at war with himself. On one hand, he'd negotiate million-dollar deals, while dealing with his private struggle with painkillers and the concussions he'd endured as a player.

Johnson shined in Spencer's most vulnerable moments when that mask slipped, showing a man who didn't want to admit he wasn't physically or mentally okay. It's a departure from his more "tough guy" roles, giving his familiar swagger a brittle edge. He wanted more than anything to prove he still belonged in the room, but carrying the weight of not being able to play anymore was a difficult burden for him to carry at times, and Johnson portrayed that struggle with an authenticity that was truly the heartbeat of the show.

According to recent reports, the role also carried personal meaning for Johnson. When he declared the show’s cancellation on social media, he reflected on never getting the chance to play in the NFL as he once dreamed, but that Ballers gave him “the opportunity to play a character that loved the game.” That sincerity came through on-screen, especially in scenes where Spencer tried to mentor some of those players like Ricky (John David Washington), warning him not to repeat his mistakes, or when he pushed Charles (Omar Miller) to find pride in life after football. And even in his lighter moments with his boss, played by the hilarious Rob Corddry, Johnson proved he could be the center of a strong ensemble cast week to week. Add in cameos from real athletes like NBA star Steph Curry and NFL Super Bowl Champion Odell Beckham Jr., and Ballers felt authentic while still entertaining.

It has been revealed that behind the camera, the show solidified Johnson’s multi-hyphenate status. Serving as an executive producer alongside Mark Wahlberg, he proved he could shepherd a project as well as headline it, which is a skill set that paved the way for his current role shaping entire franchises. The show’s reach even extended into politics, with Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren famously naming it her favorite series during her 2019 presidential campaign because of the way it spotlighted real-world issues facing athletes. It was proof not only of Johnson’s broad appeal, but also of the show’s surprisingly sharp storytelling.

Industry observers note that looking back, Ballers should have been much bigger, especially given Johnson’s popularity at the time, but for whatever reason, it flew a little under the radar. Today, it’s often remembered as one of HBO’s most underrated gems, and in a world with sports dramas like Friday Night Lights and Ted Lasso, it deserves to be mentioned among the best of the genre. More importantly, it became the perfect vehicle for Dwayne Johnson to prove he was more than just a global movie star and gave him the chance to stretch as an actor, grow as a producer, and show audiences a side of himself they hadn’t seen before.

According to recent reports, and in many ways, it laid the groundwork for roles like The Smashing Machine, but its five-season run is worth revisiting on its own terms. The deals and scandals keep things moving, while Spencer’s struggles give you a reason to keep watching.

Sources indicate that even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler stated. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

According to recent reports, but while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

It has been revealed that “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he remarked. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

2000-2010 was a transformative decade for sitcoms, bridging the gap between traditional multi-camera comedies and the more experimental, character-driven highlights that would define the 2010s. While network hits like Friends and Everybody Loves Raymond carried over their ratings dominance from the '90s into the early 2000s, a new generation of sitcoms challenged the genre's established conventions.

Industry observers note that throughout the decade, sitcoms increasingly embraced unconventional storytelling, surreal humor, and more complicated protagonists. Shows like The Office and Curb Your Enthusiasm helped popularize mockumentary techniques and cringe comedy. Other sitcoms experimented with serialized storytelling, genre-blending, and narrative structures that rewarded attentive viewers. These innovations helped lay the groundwork for the increasingly ambitious sitcoms of the 2010s.

The 2000s also produced some remarkably prescient social satire. Comedy could explore cultural anxieties that would only become more relevant with time. Corporate greed, celebrity obsession, technological advancement, and changing social expectations provided fertile ground for comedies whose observations now feel surprisingly contemporary.

However, the most successful sitcoms of the 2000s haven’t always aged well, like Two and a Half Men. Meanwhile, DVD box sets and reruns allowed audiences to discover overlooked comedies, while indicates that struggled during their original runs developed cult followings and earned critical reevaluation. Some even received unexpected revivals years after their cancellations.

Industry observers note that ultimately, the 2000s sitcoms that have aged like fine wine weren’t necessarily considered the biggest, funniest, or even the best during their original run. Some were timeless from the beginning, while others were so far ahead of their time that audiences are only now fully appreciating them.

Sources indicate that scrubs was beloved during its original run, but its blend of surrealist comedy and emotional realism has become even more distinctive. While J.D.'s elaborate daydreams provided absurdist humor, Scrubs embraced truly sad episodes, never shying away from the grief, burnout, and moral dilemmas that come with working in a life-or-death profession.

Recent findings suggest that more importantly, it recognized that humor wasn't a distraction from those experiences, but a necessary coping mechanism for healthcare workers. That understanding has helped the show remain perennially popular, leading to the 2026 Scrubs revival that feels like a natural continuation rather than an exercise in nostalgia.

The Bernie Mac Show was ahead of its time in its refreshingly unconventional portrayal of Black family life. Rather than depicting an idealized father figure, Bernie Mac played an impatient, frequently overwhelmed guardian who reluctantly takes in his sister's three children.

Breaking the fourth wall to address the audience directly, the show explores resentment, discipline, and the sacrifices of raising children. This feels particularly relevant as contemporary family comedies increasingly embrace imperfect caregivers and nontraditional households. Its use of direct-to-camera confessionals and uncomfortable family truths also anticipated the mockumentary storytelling that would become a sitcom staple later in the years to come.

My Name Is Earl has only gotten better with age, especially in its refreshingly optimistic approach to redemption and accountability. At a time when television increasingly embraced morally bankrupt antiheroes, Earl Hickey was something of an anti-antihero: a petty criminal determined to become a better person by making amends for his past mistakes.

Rather than mocking its working-class characters for their shortcomings, the sitcom treated them with genuine empathy, recognizing that even deeply flawed people are capable of change. Its emphasis on personal responsibility, forgiveness, and second chances feels especially refreshing in an era of increasingly polarized moral judgments.

Recent findings suggest that my Name Is Earl’s unresolved cliffhanger ending remains a bitter aftertaste. However, the show's underlying philosophy has aged beautifully.

Girlfriends was groundbreaking during its original run, but its portrayal of Black female friendship has only become more significant with time. Following four women as they navigate careers, relationships, and personal growth in Los Angeles, the sitcom challenged the limited roles available to Black women on television without reducing its characters to stereotypes.

In a recent development, more than two decades later, Girlfriends feels like a precursor to shows such as Insecure, particularly in its exploration of professional ambition, sexual independence, and complicated female friendships. Its frank discussions of Black womanhood also remain strikingly relevant, demonstrating how many of the social pressures its characters confronted have persisted long after Girlfriends' series finale.

Arrested Development is the definitive example of a sitcom that found a larger audience after its cancellation. The comedy struggled with ratings during its run, only to become a cult phenomenon through DVD sales and streaming. Arrested Development reshaped American sitcoms — its densely layered jokes, elaborate callbacks, unreliable narration, and interconnected storylines were practically designed for binge-watching.

Beyond its innovative storytelling, Arrested Development's satire of a wealthy, self-absorbed family whose privilege repeatedly shields them from consequences feels increasingly relevant. Two decades later, the Bluth family's entitlement and spectacular incompetence have only become satirically sharper with time.

Aliens in America was arguably a decade ahead of its time, tackling Islamophobia, xenophobia, and cultural prejudice through the unlikely premise of a teenage sitcom. Premiering in 2007, the short-lived comedy followed Raja, a Pakistani Muslim exchange student who moves in with a Wisconsin family expecting someone else entirely.

Rather than making Raja the punchline, Aliens in America frequently turned its humor toward the ignorance and prejudices of his American hosts, challenging stereotypes while remaining genuinely funny. At a time when hit dramas like 24 routinely associated Muslim characters with terrorism, Aliens in America pushed back against American ignorance and Islamophobia.

It has been revealed that winning three consecutive Outstanding Comedy Emmys, 30 Rock was a masterpiece but never a mainstream ratings juggernaut. When the sitcom entered its final season in 2012, it had roughly one-third the audience of The Massive Bang Theory.

However, its cultural footprint has grown considerably. The comedy's rapid-fire jokes, obscure pop culture references, background gags, and elaborate callbacks reward repeat viewing, making 30 Rock particularly well-suited to the streaming era.

Meanwhile, its relentless satire of media consolidation, celebrity branding, and corporate interference in entertainment has become increasingly prescient. What was once an industry-insider comedy now feels like a remarkably accurate portrait of modern Hollywood.

Peep Show has created an enduring cultural legacy through its painfully relatable portrayal of social anxiety and arrested adulthood. Following two dysfunctional roommates perpetually struggling to be adults, Peep Show is an anti-sitcom that took cringe comedy to uncomfortable latest heights.

Its innovative first-person camerawork and internal monologues exposed the disconnect between its characters' outward behavior and private thoughts, trapping viewers inside the insecurities and selfish impulses behind their humiliating decisions. This psychological realism anticipated the painfully self-aware humor of shows like Fleabag.

Industry observers note that more than two decades after its premiere, Peep Show's examination of social awkwardness, self-sabotage, and the inability to get one's life together feels more relevant than ever. Like a bold red wine, it might make you pucker at first, but those with a sophisticated palate will appreciate its complexity.

The Boondocks is an animated sitcom whose biting satire of American society feels just as relevant two decades after its premiere. Following brothers Huey and Riley Freeman as they navigate life in a predominantly white suburb, the Adult Swim comedy fearlessly tackles racism, politics, consumerism, and celebrity worship.

Sources indicate that rather than limiting its criticism to white America, The Boondocks also challenged contradictions within Black popular culture, particularly the glorification of violence, materialism, and fame. Its episodes satirizing sensationalist media coverage, celebrity scandals, and the commercialization of Black identity often feel almost prophetic.

Set within the morally bankrupt corporation Veridian Dynamics, Better Off Ted satirized corporate greed, unethical innovation, and the prioritization of profits over people. Nothing better illustrates how far ahead of its time the show was than its infamous “Racial Sensitivity” episode, where the organization devises increasingly ridiculous workarounds rather than fixing the technology that can’t recognize Black employees.

What seemed like absurdist satire in 2009 now feels like a remarkably accurate critique of corporate irresponsibility and reliance on flawed technology. ABC canceled Better Off Ted after two seasons, but there was plenty of juice left. Underappreciated during its original run, Better Off Ted is one of the best obscure sitcoms that everyone should watch.

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump stated his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

Industry observers note that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Crucial Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

It has been revealed that trump stated his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

It has been revealed that the bill’s sponsors unveiled more than 60 newly introduced House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

In a recent development, “Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she remarked in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

Sources indicate that A floor vote has yet to be confirmed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

Sources indicate that for crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s fresh Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

In a recent development, the criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Key Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

In a recent development, at first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

It has been revealed that that defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

“It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”.

Sources indicate that by Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more promptly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”.

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

It has been revealed that the latest installment of The Hunger Games has arrived, and audiences have spoken. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the second prequel in Suzanne Collins' popular YA dystopian franchise, and it didn't sit well with critics upon release. But what about audiences? Now that the movie has entered theaters, the viewers have spoken about their return to Panem.

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place 24 years before the events of the first Hunger Games story, during the 2nd Quarter Quell, a special Hunger Games with new rules added every 25 years to remind the districts of their defeat in the rebellion. This is the game Haymitch Abernathy participated in, now played by Joseph Zada, and the new rules for this Hunger Games were that each district would send double the number of tributes, increasing the total from 24 to 48 children in the arena.

It has been revealed that when the critics' score came out, Sunrise on the Reaping debuted with a 74% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, and as of writing, the number has dropped to 67%. However, now that the movie has entered theaters, audiences disagree, and it sits at a 95% Verified Hot Audience Score. Audience reception was also positive on Letterboxd, with the film earning a 4.1-star rating. Collider's Victoria Luxford gave Sunrise on the Reaping an 8/10 score in her review. She praised the movie's "dark and gritty" portrayal of Collins' world but criticized the runtime, especially for those "not heavily invested" in the series.

Sources indicate that ever since The Hunger Games film franchise began in 2012, six films have been released: four main movies and two prequels. According to Rotten Tomatoes critics' scores, the highest-rated Hunger Games movie is the sequel, The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, with a 90% score, followed by the first Hunger Games movie at 85%. And despite Sunrise on the Reaping's low critics' score, the lowest-rated Hunger Games movie from critics is the first prequel film, The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, with a 64% rating.

Audiences, however, viewed the franchise differently: Sunrise on the Reaping is the audience's highest-rated Hunger Games movie ever, followed by Catching Fire with an 89% rating, then the first Hunger Games movie with an 81% audience score. The audience's lowest-rated installment is The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2, with an audience score of 66% on Rotten Tomatoes.

According to recent reports, the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now showing in theaters. Follow Collider for more updates.

Taking place in Panem 24 years prior to the original series, this upcoming Hunger Games entry focuses on the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games.
